sections.h2: Where to take a deed or mortgage for recording
sections.html:
The Register of Deeds is in Suite 400 of the Purdy Building, 125 W. Lincoln Street, Caro, MI 48723. It opens at 8:00 a.m. and closes at 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, with a lunch closure from noon until 1:00 p.m., and it shuts for holidays. Call 989-672-3840 or write to registerofdeeds@tuscolacounty.org.

You can walk a document in or send it by mail. A mailed packet needs the exact fee and a stamped return envelope. Cash, money orders and checks are all taken. Checks must print both the account holder's name and the bank's name and address, and they cannot be stale-dated. A wrong amount gets the whole request rejected, so count twice before sealing the envelope.

Caro is the county seat, and the county lies in Michigan's Thumb. Recording is the final step of a sale, so confirm with your title company who is carrying the deed to the counter and when.

A single $30.00 charge covers entering and recording a deed, mortgage, lis pendens, certified copy or other instrument. Papers that discharge or assign several older records add to it.

Tuscola County recording and copy fees
ServiceCharge
Recording one instrument (deed, mortgage, lis pendens and similar)$30.00 flat
Every extra liber and page assigned, discharged, indexed or posted$3.00 extra
Photocopy, real estate record$1.00 a page
Certifying a copy$5.00 a document
Tax lien search certificate, state or federal$3.00 a name

Four dollars of every recording fee funds the Michigan State Survey and Remonumentation program. Fixture filings, lien documents, state deeds, plats and tax reversion papers skip that portion. Copies are paid for at the time of purchase, and a mailed order must give the liber and page. Fixture filings are recorded here at $30.00, while UCC filings go to the Secretary of State instead of Caro.

sections.h2: Why a warranty deed visits the Treasurer first
sections.html:
State law (MCLA 211.135) requires proof that taxes are paid before some papers reach the recorder. Three types go to the Tuscola County Treasurer first: warranty deeds, land contract assignments with a warranty clause, and condominium master deeds. The Treasurer's certification costs $5.00 per document.

When the stamped document comes back, send it on to Caro in recording order with the exact fee. The Treasurer, at the same street address, answers certification questions at 989-672-3890.

Sellers carrying unpaid tax feel this step most. Settle early with your title company or closing attorney, who will order the certificate, since each mailed round trip adds days to a closing.

sections.h2: Paperwork mistakes that get a recording returned?
sections.html:
Staff check each submission against the Recording Requirements list, which starts from MCL 565.201. A document that misses any item goes back to the sender.

  • Original signatures, each with the signer's name typed or printed beneath it. Fax and photocopy versions are refused.
  • An acknowledgement by a notary, judge or court clerk on any paper that conveys or burdens Michigan land.
  • A mailing address for every grantee, plus the name and address of whoever drafted the paper.
  • Black print of 10 points or larger on white paper between letter and legal size, leaving a blank 2 1/2 inches atop page one and 1/2 inch on other margins.
  • No more than four sequential Social Security digits anywhere on the page.
  • One recordable event per instrument, named on the first line of print.

Court orders and death certificates are recordable only as certified copies, and a survivor deed needs the death certificate recorded or referenced by liber and page. Staff do not draft deeds, answer legal questions or hand out blank forms, so use an attorney or title company for wording.

sections.h2: Transfer tax on a recorded deed
sections.html:
Recording a sale brings two charges. The county's is in MCL 207.504: 55 cents per $500 of value, with any leftover under $500 counted as a full unit, for counties below 2,000,000 people. The state's is in MCL 207.525, at $3.75 for each $500 or fraction.

Value must appear on the face of the deed or in an attached affidavit. The whole consideration is taxed unless the paper cites a valid exemption.

  • Both acts exempt consideration under $100, security instruments, leases and certain land contracts.
  • The state act, MCL 207.526, adds conveyances from an individual to a child, stepchild, grandchild or step-grandchild, plus foreclosure transfers.
  • The county act's list, MCL 207.505, lacks the family exemption. Ask the office how the county share applies when a parent deeds a house to a child.

Online indexes start in December 1988, and the vault holds land records back to 1852 for visitors. Every index is by grantor and grantee name. There is no search by street address or parcel number, and the office keeps land records only, so it cannot tell you a build date.

Copies of recorded documents are open to anyone, since recording makes them public. Residents can sign up for Property Alert, an email notice whenever a paper under their name is recorded. It works as a heads-up, and a common name will trigger false alarms. If an alert shows a document you do not recognize, phone the office.

Staff run only simple searches for a small fee and cannot say who owns a parcel. An attorney or title company reaches that conclusion.

sections.h2: Selling when the property taxes are behind
sections.html:
The Tuscola County Treasurer works with delinquent owners to head off foreclosure and lays out three paths: keep the property, sell it, or let foreclosure proceed. Forfeiture comes first and is not foreclosure. During it, the county adds a title search fee of at least $175 plus recording costs, and interest climbs to 18% a year (1.5% monthly), reaching back to the start of the delinquency.

A year after forfeiture, foreclosure follows. The owner's interest and every lien are wiped out, redemption ends, and the parcel is prepared for auction. Listings usually appear in early August for the August and October auctions. For a bill you dispute, or for a Principal Residence, veteran or hardship exemption, call your township assessor.

Selling before forfeiture is the cheaper route. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff, pay it from proceeds at closing, and the Treasurer's certificate can issue so the warranty deed records on schedule. A cash sale works the same way and can close fast, as long as the payoff is settled.

Homeownership in the county is high at 86.4%, and the median owner-occupied value is $149,500.

faqs.q: What will a Tuscola County recording cost me?
faqs.a: Expect $30.00 flat per instrument, with $3.00 more for each extra liber and page. Transfer tax comes on top, figured on the total consideration unless the document states an exemption.

faqs.q: Does a Tuscola County warranty deed need a tax certificate first?
faqs.a: Yes. Send the document to the Tuscola County Treasurer first with the $5.00 certification fee, then submit the stamped document to the Register of Deeds with exact recording fees. The Treasurer's phone is 989-672-3890.

faqs.q: Can a Tuscola County deed be found by street address?
faqs.a: No. Indexing is by name only. Search by grantor or grantee, or bring the liber and page. Online indexes start December 1, 1988.

faqs.q: Who may order a copy of a Tuscola County deed?
faqs.a: Anyone may. Each page costs $1.00, certifying a copy adds $5.00 per document, and a mailed order needs a self-addressed stamped envelope.

faqs.q: Which transfer tax rates apply to a Tuscola County sale?
faqs.a: The county charges 55 cents and the state $3.75, each for every $500 of value. The value comes from the instrument or an attached affidavit.
